item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) Keep Him In The Dark
item.content:encoded:
Called by PM

+ show block
– hide block

So my concern here is that you’ve written yourself into a corner. SCP travels between dimensions, but doesn’t know. He can’t know. And in all of those dimensions he’s contained by the foundation.

The first thing I’d say is if the multiple foundation variants are aware that he’s going from containment cell to containment cell and not really aware of it, they could just leave well enough alone. Why try to stop his shifting? As long as the containment protocols are in place, he wouldn’t be able to breach in a traditional sense at all.

Second thing, because he’s just flitting from one containment cell to the next, this isn’t the most exciting of ideas. You can’t do wild stories because his life is prettt much always the same. AND because he doesn’t know, you also can’t develop his feelings about the matter because part of the premise is he’s ignorant.

Finally, it sorta beggars belief that all seven foundations have information sharing to the point where they have parallel files on him that are updated accordingly.

All in all, this seems like a much dryer version of the Unwilling Dimension Hopper skip from early on…

Without a completely rewritten concept at its core, I don’t know that this article would survive as you propose it currently.

item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) Keep Him In The Dark

Hopefully this will both add a bit of foreshadowing for the final log, and give us some more insight into the researchers assigned to the SCP.

Hopefully this will add a more interesting element on the part of the researchers attempting to work with him.

Like there's kinda a progression through the logs with the events getting more severe and the foundation eventually changing track to try a different approach; but it feels…unguided? I think what this really needs is like…a central character or group of characters who like are in charge of handling the outcome of each of the incidents and with like, trying stuff to reduce their severity; perhaps with the overall angle being something like "their initial attempts failed because they didn't work with the SCP and it was only together they succeeded" kinda thing but?

It's very possible the issue is just the idea doesn't vibe with me though so like, you may want to ask a few other experienced reviewers.

item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) Keep Him In The Dark
item.content:encoded:
I am a newbie and I cannot give green-lights!
Please take my criticism with a LARGE grain of salt

This is a placeholder, I will give my thoughts as soon as I can. If I don't give a review in over 48 hours, please don't be afraid to send me a Wikidot PM. I can easily forget things.

I'm looking at your idea from a horror story-focused perspective.

+ OPEN CRIT
- CLOSE CRIT

Being too specific on anomalies, not being specific on the important parts

A humanoid SCP who unwillingly jumps between 7 parallel dimensions…

From my own experience and time of looking up good tips, why do you have to specify exactly how many dimensions the SCP goes through? From what I've read on horror, some of the best things to do is when you keep things vague and mysterious enough that the reader doesn't get the full picture.

You can say that the foundation has so far located 7 parallel dimensions of themselves, but don't make it an exact number. For instance, maybe they've only found 7 so far and aren't sure if any more exist and to what extent. This is just nitpicking, but it's important to give details like these in my opinion.

Story is not fleshed out; there's some plotholes and questions that arise

If he discovers a discontinuity, he unconsciously and automatically warps reality to match what he believes to be the baseline.

While I do understand the concept, it just doesn't sit right with me because it doesn't feel as fleshed out. The story doesn't feel well-paired with the concept and the SCP alone is quite complex from the beginning.

Things like these need to be explained or answered:

  • How does this happen, is it that is whatever is a discrepancy suddenly changes out of nowhere?
  • Does the SCP react in any sort of way?
  • Does the SCP know about its anomaly? You specified that he shouldn't know any discrepancies or else the universe will change, but what is to stop the Foundation from just explaining this to the SCP and having the SCP just be prepared for every switch he makes.
  • If you DO plan on having it where the foundation can't tell the SCP about his powers, then ask yourself why else would the foundation keep him understudy as an SCP if he isn't supposed to know his powers? You'd think that an SCP who is THIS dangerous and shouldn't know about it powers, would not be held in the way that it is. Maybe give some backstory into the SCP itself and how it manages to preserve this capture as normal?
  • What stops the Foundation from using simple amnestics on him to help him forget his memory?

Give more detail!

A number of incident logs in which he realizes that…
…procedures with suggestions from the SCP

See, in-general I feel that this story isn't as detailed and this is a clear example of that.
You say that there will be logs, but nothing is really specified besides some vague actions that occur within them.

Trying to fix the plothole later on; adding his awareness doesn't solve the issue

The fourth log is an interview in which the SCP is informed of it's abilities, and is asked to assist in it's own containment, especially in keeping it unaware that he's shifted.

See, you can't just fix an issue with the story's beginning by having them tell him later on within the story in this way. It's not like the SCP was just found and the Foundation only recently started testing it, this is after 3 interview logs and god-knows how many tests or studies. I'm sure they would've simply told him this stuff from the begging. This just doesn't fit right here in general and seems like a big plot-hole.

"Suggestions" aren't given by SCPs

He agrees, and the article ends with a pending request to update procedures with suggestions from the SCP.

and is asked to assist in it's own containment, especially in keeping it unaware that he's shifted.

Remember, your SCP is.. well, an SCP. The Foundation doesn't just accept SCPs' recommendations or suggestions, The Foundation only deals with what helps them in their goals and what the SCP really needs. The Foundation may REWARD your SCP for complying, but they don't simply just accept suggestions or ask nicely unless a reason is needed to do so. More of this is explained in the guide So You Want to Write a Humanoid SCP Object (which I highly suggest you read if you want this to work).

Improving by simply reading other's work

From what I can tell, although this is just an assumption, I presume your SCP is inspired by SCP-507? While I do get that maybe you haven't read it, both seem earily similar with a few changes and less depictions. I recommend reading through it, looking at the similarities or how that document did it well, and then figuring out how you can differentiate yourself from it.

I also highly recommend reading some of the most recent SCP articles and seeing what they do right, in order to help flesh out your idea. This way, you can become familiar with the style while also understanding *how* to help out with your goals on this SCP.

BIGGEST PIECE OF ADVICE I CAN GIVE YOU

Where is the Horror?

Genre (Optional): Horror…

I don't see any real horror going on with this story. So, to allow horror or terror to be given from an article, it's good to keep things vague, mysterious, or thought-provoking. For people to feel horror in your narrative, there has to be something they can relate to and also not-understand.

I HIGHLY recommend looking at some of the most recent articles for this, as the style of horror and SCP articles in-general appears to have changed over the span of years. SCP-096 for instance, although terrifying in its own right, wouldn't be accepted in the same way as if it were to be published today.

Some articles I know that are really useful for understanding this are…
'Things what do a thing'- An Essay On Anomalies That Are Things That Do A Thing
So You Want to Write a Humanoid SCP Object
Horror writing tips. (Read Hornby's reply on 12 Jul 2012, 19:36)
Dr. Mackenzie's Documentation Tips

Give it more story!

Genre (Optional): …Drama/Emotional

WHY should I care about discrepancies in the universe?
WHY should I care about multiple versions of the Foundation working together?
WHAT is the SCP's backstory?
WHAT feelings do the Foundation staff show, if any at all?
WHAT are the specifics in the details you're giving us?
HOW is this story something I can really get the sense of "I got a general picture, but there's still a ton I'm unsure about?" (Horror aspect)
WHERE is the emotional connection with the characters?

A good piece of advise would be for you to list out your events, all in order, while specifying how the Foundation, the Staff, the SCP, react to the event you're playing out to them.

FINAL THOUGHTS AND SUMMARY

TLDR:

  • Be more vague on the SCP's anomalies and other factors to increase thought-provoktion and horror
  • Flesh out your story in-general
  • Give more detail to parts of your story
  • Fix the suggestion/recommendtion bits
  • Improve by reading other authors' work
  • Give it more horror
  • Give it more story

My Overall/Final Thoughts

This idea just doesn't seem to work. I'm glad you put so much effort and time into getting critique into this concept, but I just don't feel like it'll work out.

My best advice to you is just scrap the idea and start working on a new idea all together. Use all the critique and advice you had gotten from this one to help you with its creation.

Don't let it wear you down. Not every idea lands, (I learned the hard way around 3 times now), and the best you can do is try to spend more time on making an even better idea than this one.

Good luck to you! Glad I was able to critique this.

item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) Keep Him In The Dark
item.content:encoded:
I think the big thing that I didn't portray well enough in the original post, and will try to correct, is that the activation of the powers is almost completely unconscious and automatic. If he notices a change, he simply causes the change to no longer be there. The only way to stop it is for him to not notice changes, hence the constant monitoring and goal of keeping the various containments synced.

I agree that the narrative is a bit shallow and late. The new focus is much more on the foundation attempting to gaslight him so even if he does notice the changes, he thinks they're more in his own head, rather than reality being different. I also think the logs will be shorter and much more focused than I first intended. I've reworked the post to show the current idea for the chain of events, which should be a lot more definite and specific.

item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) Keep Him In The Dark
item.content:encoded:
Ok, I think I wasn't as clear as I could be. I'll try to adjust the post accordingly. The ability to bring realities back in line is unconscious and automatic beyond the fact that he has to notice a difference for it to kick in. The moment he notices a difference, he causes the difference to go away. Furthermore, he can't warp reality to any degree beyond adjusting his current one to what he believes is the baseline. The reality warping is dependent on him having moved from one dimension to another.

I've updated the original post with a more specific and focused version of the story. The focus is less on the character's growth, and more on the idea of the foundation gaslighting them in a poor attempt to contain them.

item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) Keep Him In The Dark
item.content:encoded:
In general, your core element's anomalies should make sense when considered altogether. Unconnected anomalous qualities can feel disconnected and confusing for a reader; a platypus that speaks French and poops iPhones is going to be considerably more difficult to fit in a story than, say, a surfer who can talk to dolphins.

How would that arc be represented in the rest of the article? A final interview can certainly help cement emotional growth, but we need to see how that growth began in the first place. cybersqyd puts it much better than I could below.

[+] Open for crit
– hide block

A number of incident logs in which he realizes that the world around him has changed, and warps reality to change it back.

So like, what do these actually look like? My concern is that you're in a situation where they don't add a lot individually but they're also not really hugely interesting; and so you both want short logs to not dwell on them much but also longer logs to really try and show why they are interesting; and neither option quite works.

culminating in an interview in which he is finally informed of his abilities, and chooses to assist the foundation in making sure he is unaware of when he shifts, especially after reflecting on the harm he's caused.

so like, this is fine but like…if he realises he's caused a lot of harm, and there's implication he's in full control of his reality bending abilities, why does he need to be kept unaware of when shifts occur? Surely he can just like…understand that is what is going on and not get mad?

More to the point, why does he even alter reality? Like I get him wanting to shift stuff back towards what it should be on paper but it doesn't seem like there's any changes that actually materially affect him since he's in foundation containment in all the cases and there's not like a big driving force like "my wife died in 6/7 of the realities and i want her to be around still"?

I think my big concern is that the narrative arc feels excessively shallow and very late: the actual growth of the SCP doesn't kick in until the final act when he's told about the reality bending powers and then it immediately all happens then; and it feels like the earlier incident logs just…are filler material to bridge the gap instead of like, actually adding to what you want to do here?

Alright, here’s my take.

+ show block
– hide block

Let’s start with a nitpick. What’s the connection between your protagonist’s dimensional jumping and their reality warping? Those are two separate and powerful anomalous abilities, and it would be nice to have an explanation for why both are present in a single entity.

I’m having issues figuring out what your actual arc is here. What changes from the beginning of the narrative to the end? For that matter, how should the reader feel about that change? Part of the concern when it comes to articles that focus on unique forms of containment is that if everything goes well, nothing much will happen or change. This can be rather stultifying to the audience unless other, more introspective forms of growth/change become the focus.

item.title: (Seeking Greenlight) Keep Him In The Dark
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Horror, Drama/Emotional

Elevator Pitch: A humanoid SCP who unwillingly jumps between 7 parallel dimensions, in all of which he is in foundation custody. The goal of the containment procedures are to make him believe he is living in a singular reality, by adjusting his cell, keeping personnel up to date on activities, etc. If he discovers a discontinuity, he unconsciously and automatically warps reality to match what he believes to be the baseline. The parallel foundations communicate via a wireless device that he is able to bring with him.

Central Narrative: A number of incident logs in which he realizes that the world around him has changed, and warps reality to change it back. Symptoms of this involve causing personnel who died in the previous reality to die in the current one and shifts in personality of personnel along the same lines. The first log incident is a member of site staff who died in one of the parallel dimensions talking to the SCP against orders, and being wiped from existence. The second log is an interview in which foundation staff attempt to convince the SCP that he's crazy, so that even if he does notice a change, he might believe it's all in his head rather than a change in reality. The interview continues after the staff leave the interview room, with them debating whether or not what they just did was either morally or tactically correct.

At this point, there will be a denied request to change tactics, and work with the SCP. The third log documents a containment breach that started without warning, after he shifted from a dimension that was experiencing a containment breach. The earlier request is resubmitted and approved. The fourth log is an interview in which the SCP is informed of it's abilities, and is asked to assist in it's own containment, especially in keeping it unaware that he's shifted. He agrees, and the article ends with a pending request to update procedures with suggestions from the SCP.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The idea of having to keep an adult humanoid SCP unaware that it's power has activated, especially with coordination between multiple groups with extremely difficult communication. The tension comes from having to sync up quickly, and the consequences of failure. There will also be some exploration of the effects and morality of the foundation having to gaslight him constantly to maintain containment.
